author.name: Alfred J. Church
author.biography: A schoolmaster who became professor of Latin at University College London, he retold many Greek and Roman stories for young readers.

hook.text: What does one man's anger cost everyone around him?

paragraphs: For nine years a Greek army has camped outside Troy. The Trojan prince Paris carried off Helen, the wife of King Menelaus of Sparta, and the Greeks have come to take her back. They win their battles in the open field, but they cannot break through the city walls.

The story begins with a quarrel. Agamemnon, the leader of the Greeks, takes the girl Briseis from Achilles, their greatest fighter, to make up for a prize of his own that he has had to give back. Achilles withdraws from the war, and without him the battle turns: Hector, the eldest son of King Priam of Troy, drives the Greeks back toward their ships.

Between the battles come quieter scenes. Hector says goodbye to his wife Andromache and their small son on the city wall; two enemies meet between the armies and find that their families are old friends; envoys go to plead with Achilles in his tent. On Mount Olympus the gods take sides and argue among themselves.

Alfred Church retold Homer's Iliad for young readers in plain prose. It is not a translation of the Greek poem, but it keeps Homer's order of events, and like the poem it tells of a few weeks in the last year of the war, not the whole siege.

orientation.text: Twenty-four chapters, beginning with an introduction to the Greek world and its gods that also covers the Odyssey. Short lines after some paragraphs show how to say the Greek names, and the names follow older English forms such as Ulysses and Diomed.
